title: The AI Cost Curve Is Finally Becoming Visible
summary: AT&T cut its AI bill by 56%, Uber reduced cost per session by 52%, and Pinterest is running open models at less than 8% of closed model costs, all while maintaining or expanding AI usage. The shift is not toward less AI but toward deliberate routing, and the companies with the best visibility into their model stack will have a structural cost advantage over those still defaulting to frontier models for every task.
body_markdown:
For years, enterprise AI adoption has been shaped by a simple assumption: **using more AI means spending more money.**


That assumption is starting to break down.


- **AT&T** reportedly cut its AI bill by **56%** .
- **Uber** reduced the cost per AI request by **34%** and the cost per session by **52%** .
- **Pinterest** has been running open models at **less than 8% of the cost** of comparable closed proprietary models.


These examples point to the same conclusion. Enterprises are not necessarily using less AI. They are becoming more deliberate about how they use it, which models they select, and how each request is routed.


The result is a shift in the economics of AI. The question is no longer only which model is the most capable. It is also which model is appropriate for a specific task, and what that task should cost.


## Open Models and Smart Routing Are Changing the Equation


The strongest cost reductions are not coming from a single breakthrough model. They are coming from a combination of **open models and intelligent routing** .


Different AI tasks require different levels of capability. A routine classification, simple transformation, or straightforward code review may not need the most expensive frontier model available. A complex reasoning task may justify a more capable model. Routing each request to the right model creates an opportunity to reduce costs without reducing the overall quality of an AI workflow.


This is especially important for companies operating AI at scale. A small difference in the cost of one request can become a substantial saving when multiplied across millions of requests, users, or automated sessions.


Open-weight models are making this approach more practical. They offer enterprises greater control over deployment, pricing, and model selection. They can also provide a lower-cost option for high-volume workloads where the most advanced proprietary model would be excessive.


The goal is not to replace every closed model. It is to use each model where it makes the most economic and operational sense.


## Model Pricing Is Becoming a Strategic Consideration


The latest pricing differences make the shift especially clear.


For code review, the most expensive open-weight model cited in the post costs around **$0.30 per task** . That compares with approximately **$0.50** for the least expensive frontier model and **$2.50** for the most expensive one.


At the model level, the difference can be even more dramatic. Opus 5 is described as costing roughly **100 times more** than GPT-5.6 Luna xhigh or DeepSeek for the same prompt.


These are not minor variations. They represent materially different cost structures for teams building AI products and internal workflows.


When pricing varies this widely, model selection becomes part of product strategy. Engineering teams need to understand which tasks require premium reasoning, which tasks can run on smaller models, and where an open model can deliver an acceptable result at a fraction of the cost.


This also changes how companies should evaluate model performance. Benchmark leadership remains useful, but it is only one part of the equation. A model that performs slightly better but costs many times more may not be the best choice for a particular workflow.


The more useful question is often: **what level of quality does this task require, and what is the lowest-cost model that can reliably provide it?**


## Enterprise AI Spending Is Becoming More Rational


Data from Ramp suggests that AI spending fell by **10% among the top 1% of businesses** in August.


That decline does not necessarily mean these companies are losing interest in AI. It may indicate that early experimentation is giving way to more disciplined adoption.


During the first phase of AI deployment, companies often prioritize speed. Teams test multiple tools, enable new capabilities, and accept higher costs in exchange for learning quickly. Over time, finance, engineering, and operations teams begin to examine actual usage patterns.


They identify which models are being used, how often they are called, which workflows generate the most value, and where costs are rising without a corresponding business benefit.


This is a natural stage in the development of any important technology. Adoption continues, but waste declines. The organization learns to distinguish between high-value AI usage and expensive experimentation.


For enterprise leaders, this means **AI cost management should not be treated as a last-minute optimization exercise** . It should be built into the architecture from the beginning.


## The Next Advantage Will Come From Control


The broader lesson is that AI economics are moving closer to reality.


For a period, many companies were willing to accept unclear or heavily subsidized pricing while the market developed. Now, usage-based billing, model diversity, and more detailed cost data are making the actual economics easier to see.


The companies that benefit most will not necessarily be the ones using the largest models for every task. They will be the ones with the best **visibility and control over their AI stack** .


That means selecting models based on workload requirements, routing requests intelligently, using open models where they fit, and measuring the cost of each workflow.


Enterprise adopters are not stepping away from AI. They are learning to pay closer attention to what it actually costs.


**The future of AI may be defined not by using more intelligence at any price, but by delivering the right intelligence at the right cost.**
